title: Network steering with arbitrarily low detection efficiency of any entangled measurement
abstract: Quantum nonlocality and its asymmetric counterpart, quantum steering, are among the most intriguing manifestations of quantum mechanics. From a theoretical perspective, they are not only of fundamental significance but also hold promise for a wide range of applications. However, the stringent technological requirements for their experimental observation in a loophole-free way have largely restricted their realization to foundational demonstrations. A major challenge in these setups is the limited detection efficiency of current detectors as to observe nonlocality or steering in the standard scenarios, one requires detectors above a certain critical efficiency which can only be achieved with superconducting detectors. Considering the simplest quantum network, we demonstrate here that quantum steering between two parties, can be demonstrated for any non-zero detection efficiency, if the sources in the network generate states above a critical visibility well-within the current practical limits. This form of quantum steering in networks, is termed swap-steering. Moreover, when the sources are perfect, swap-steering can be observed using any entangled measurement on the untrusted side, even with arbitrarily low detection efficiency. Consequently, two major loopholes, the detection-loophole as well as free-will loophole can be closed easily in quantum steering experiments, when implemented using networks.
summary: This paper develops a protocol, termed 'swap-steering,' to demonstrate quantum steering in network settings. It overcomes the major experimental hurdle of low detector efficiency by showing that the required violation can be detected even with imperfect detectors, provided the sources have sufficient visibility. This significantly advances the feasibility of loophole-free quantum nonlocality tests.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of demonstrating quantum steering (asymmetric nonlocality) in a loophole-free manner, particularly when limited by low detector efficiency.
main_result: Quantum steering can be demonstrated for any non-zero detection efficiency using a 'swap-steering' protocol, and if sources are perfect, this can be achieved even with arbitrarily low detection efficiency.
method: The authors construct and analyze 'swap-steering witnesses' to detect quantum steering by comparing predicted correlations against bounds derived from a Source-Only-Hidden-State (SOHS) model.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum networks involving two parties (Alice and Bob) receiving subsystems from multiple classically correlated sources. The core model is the swap-steering scenario.
key_observables: Swap-steering inequality value ($S_{\{E_b\}}$), detection efficiency ($\eta$), and source visibility ($v$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the correlations can be bounded by an SOHS model, and the initial challenge is overcoming the requirement for high-efficiency detectors.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates witnessing entanglement in measurements using multiple trusted sources, and Figure 2 illustrates the swap-steering setup involving multiple sources.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework for witnessing steering using witnesses, then develops the swap-steering inequality by comparing quantum predictions to SOHS bounds, culminating in the demonstration that the inequality can be violated under realistic, low-efficiency conditions.
why_interesting: It provides a robust theoretical framework for loophole-free quantum tests that can be implemented using current, imperfect technology, which is highly relevant for experimental quantum information science.

To de- tect entanglement in the measurement acting on N subsys- tems, one needs to consider N independent trusted sources that generate local states and send them to the untrusted mea- surement. From the obtained statistics, one can infer whether the measurement has entanglement or not.

FIG. 2. Swap-steering scenario. Alice and Bob are spatially separated and each of them receives N subsystems from the untrusted sources. On the received subsystem Bob performs a single measurement while Alice being trusted performs a to- mography on her subsystem. From the experiment, they ob- tain the correlations {p(a, b|i1 . . . iN)}.
